deck.headline: S&P 500 and Dow enter correction as Nasdaq drops 5.3% and Nvidia sinks 14%
deck.sub: An SEC accounting probe at Nvidia, Anthropic's 8.5% second-day fall and fears over AI spending sent markets from Taipei to New York sharply lower.
deck.summary: US stocks fell sharply on Friday. The Nasdaq dropped 5.3% and the S&P 500 3.7%, which with the Dow's 1.9% fall puts both in a correction. Nvidia lost about 14% after a report that the SEC is examining its accounting, and Anthropic fell 8.5% on its second day. Taiwan lost more than 17% over the week.
deck.whyItMatters: This is now a broad market correction, not just an AI-stock wobble; banks with exposure to data-centre loans, GPU-backed credit and margin lending should check collateral values and concentration this week.
deck.checked: Nasdaq Composite close checked on Nasdaq's own index data (opened); S&P 500, Dow, Nvidia, ANT, 10-year and bitcoin closes from Yahoo Finance market data (opened); correction and Asia moves from the BBC (opened)
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI stocks and market mood · day 2
deck.detailHtml:
Friday turned a bad week for AI stocks into a correction. Nasdaq's own data show the Nasdaq Composite closed at 22,617.73, down 1,261 points (5.28%). The S&P 500 fell 3.7% to 6,910.39 and the Dow 1.9% to 48,147.33; the BBC says both are now 10% or more below their recent highs. Nvidia fell about 14% to $125.53, its worst day since the January 2025 DeepSeek rout, after Reuters reported that the SEC's probe is examining its accounting (see the Nvidia card). Anthropic closed its second day at $88.91, down 8.5%, after dipping to about $85, close to its $83 IPO price. Tesla and SpaceX fell more than 7.6%, Meta more than 5%. Asia went first: Taiwan fell about 6%, taking its weekly fall past 17%, and the Kospi and Nikkei about 5%. Europe fell less (DAX -2.6%, FTSE -1%). Investors bought bonds: the US 10-year yield fell to 4.91% from 5.05%. Bitcoin touched $57,716, its lowest since September 2024.

Three things hit at once. The first is Nvidia: Reuters reported that the SEC's investigation, first reported by the WSJ on Tuesday, is looking at its accounting, and the company has already delayed its quarterly 10-Q. Nvidia lost about $485bn in value on Friday and nearly $900bn on the week. The second is Anthropic: the first listed frontier lab gave back half its first-day gain, a sign that even a successful IPO cannot reset the mood. The third is politics: since the Democrats' midterm wins, investors have priced in tougher rules on data centres, and on Thursday the Senate passed a bill making them pay more for grid upgrades (see the energy card).

The moves in Asia were bigger than in New York. Taiwan, home of TSMC, has lost more than 17% in a week, which the BBC says is reported as its worst week since 1990. Memory makers SK Hynix, Kioxia and Tokyo Electron led Korea and Japan lower. Bonds rallied, which takes some pressure off borrowers, but credit spreads on AI-linked debt are the number to watch next week: the ECB warned on Wednesday that debt-funded data centres could carry an equity correction into credit markets.

deck.headline: Anthropic mathematician says Claude helped him prove the Riemann Hypothesis
deck.sub: Levent Alpöge released a machine-checkable proof that experts have only begun to check; a separate human proof appeared the same day.
deck.summary: Anthropic mathematician Levent Alpöge says he and an internal Claude model proved the Riemann Hypothesis and its generalised form, with a machine-checkable Lean proof. Terence Tao says checking it will take time. The same day, a separate all-human proof by Stanford's Alessandro Masullo was posted. Neither has been verified yet.
deck.whyItMatters: If it holds, an AI system has helped settle the most famous open problem in mathematics; until the Lean files are independently built and the statement checked, treat it as a strong claim, not a result.
deck.checked: Claim read in Alpöge's own note (opened); Tao's and Aaronson's posts and Vakil's announcement opened; BBC opened; the Lean proof itself not checked by us
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI doing mathematics · day 3
deck.detailHtml: In a two-page note posted on 20 Nov, Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, writes: 'I believe I have, working with Claude, discovered a proof of the Riemann Hypothesis', adding that the method extends to the Generalized Riemann Hypothesis (GRH) and that 'Claude and I have also formalized the arguments without assumptions' in Lean, a language computers use to check proofs. The BBC says the work took about six weeks with a non-public Claude model; Scott Aaronson puts the Lean code at 17.4 million lines (the BBC says over 250,000), released as 14 archive files. Terence Tao calls it an 'enormous' Lean-only proof whose strategy 'appears to use the full power of modern developments on the Langlands program' and says digesting it 'will take some time'. Hours later, Stanford's Ravi Vakil posted a separate, all-human proposed GRH proof by Alessandro Masullo, which Brian Conrad has been checking for months. Tao also lists AI-assisted, Lean-checked proofs that the 3D Euler and Navier-Stokes equations can blow up in finite time, by Alpöge, Tristan Buckmaster and Matei Coiculescu.

deck.headline: Trump says US firms will not be allowed to build AI data centres abroad
deck.sub: He threatened a 'tremendous tax' and named Google's Finland project, but gave no detail on how a ban would work.
deck.summary: Trump said US companies will not be allowed to build AI data centres in other countries, warning that 'China will take all of them', and threatened a 'tremendous tax' on those that do. He named Google's Finland project. No policy text exists yet and he gave no detail on how it would be enforced.
deck.whyItMatters: No policy exists yet, but lenders and investors in overseas AI campuses (Gulf, Nordics, Canada, South-East Asia, India) now carry a new US political risk that should be priced into project finance.
deck.checked: Quotes checked on the BBC (opened); also reported by NBC and ABC affiliates
deck.storyline: Storyline: building AI's power and data centres · day 30
deck.detailHtml: Back from Asia, Donald Trump told reporters on 20 Nov: 'We're not going to allow our companies to build data centres outside of our country, because China will take all of them.' He threatened a 'tremendous tax' on firms that do, said his cabinet was hearing the idea for the first time, and called out Google's €13bn Finland investment. The BBC notes Meta is building in Alberta and Anthropic has agreed to lease a planned site in Nova Scotia. It comes days after Commerce made buyers of advanced chips abroad get licences.

deck.headline: Nvidia sinks 14% as the SEC reportedly examines its accounting
deck.summary: Nvidia shares fell about 14% on Friday after Reuters reported that the SEC's investigation is looking at its accounting. The company lost about $900 billion in value this week, its worst week since 2008. Its quarterly filing is delayed, and Treasury wants answers from its board within ten days.
deck.whyItMatters: An accounting question at the company that anchors AI capex turns a valuation scare into a credibility test; lenders with Nvidia-linked collateral should watch the 10-Q date closely.
deck.update: Reuters reports the SEC probe is examining Nvidia's accounting; the stock fell about 14% on Friday, its worst week since October 2008
deck.storyline: Storyline: who runs Nvidia · day 9
deck.detailHtml: Nvidia fell about 14% on 20 Nov to $125.53, its seventh straight loss and worst day since January 2025, after Reuters reported that the SEC probe first reported by the WSJ on Tuesday is examining potential accounting issues. It lost about $485bn in value on the day and nearly $900bn on the week, its worst week since October 2008, and has lost about $2.7 trillion since its 6 Oct record; it now ranks fourth in the US by value (Yahoo Finance, Dow Jones data). Nvidia has said its 10-Q will come 'in the coming weeks' and mentioned an independent board committee investigation. Open questions include about $104bn of 2025 revenue booked through its Singapore unit (FT), the customer Megaspeed, and receivables of 64 days of sales, the most since 2022. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said this week he wants answers from the board 'in the next 10 days'. Nvidia and the SEC did not comment.

deck.headline: Arizona opens a criminal probe into OpenAI over rogue AI agents in banks
deck.summary: Arizona's attorney general has opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI and other AI firms over what she called the infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents. Separately, Citi changed its terms so customers are responsible for anything a third-party AI agent does in their account, even if the agent is hacked.
deck.whyItMatters: Liability for agent-initiated transactions is being set by state prosecutors and bank terms, not by a federal rule; banks need clear agent policies, detection and customer disclosures now.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI agents and financial firms · day 6
deck.detailHtml: Arizona Attorney General Kris Mayes said on 18 Nov that her office has opened a criminal investigation into OpenAI and other AI companies she would not name over the 'apparent infiltration of banks by rogue AI agents' (Reuters via Insurance Journal). She has spoken to Arizona banks but did not name them. It follows California's lawsuit against OpenAI two days earlier. Banks are also moving on their own: Citi's new online terms, added this month, say that if customers give a third-party AI agent their credentials, Citi will treat everything the agent does as authorised by the customer, even if it is hacked or exceeds its instructions (PYMNTS). A Dallas Fed survey found 11.4% of banks already restrict customers' AI agents and 22.9% plan to within six months.

deck.headline: Chinese hackers' AI agents found and used a zero-day on their own, Amazon says
deck.summary: Amazon says suspected Chinese spies let AI agents attack East Asian universities on their own for two days. After failing for nearly a day, the agents found a new flaw in MONAI Label, an open-source medical-imaging AI tool, and took over a server in about 11 minutes. The flaw has been fixed.
deck.whyItMatters: Patient, autonomous attackers that try for a day and then find new bugs change patch maths; open-source AI tools on internet-facing servers need the same scrutiny as web apps.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI in cyberattacks · day 23
deck.detailHtml: Amazon's chief information security officer CJ Moses says suspected Chinese spies used Cairn, an open-source AI penetration-testing framework, to let AI agents attack universities in East Asia for 48 hours from 8 Sep, with prompts in Simplified Chinese. For nearly a day the agents failed: 148 steps against a Redis server, Log4Shell and SSRF attempts, credential sprays. Then they found a path-traversal zero-day in MONAI Label, an open-source medical-imaging AI tool, and went from mapping its API to writing files on the server in about 11 minutes, taking full control. Amazon found the attacker's own Cairn server exposed online; MONAI has released a fix.

deck.headline: Bell Canada says an 'agentic' hacker stole its business customers' data
deck.summary: Bell Canada says an 'agentic' attacker, suggesting AI-driven tools, broke into several systems on 17 November, including its circuit-ordering system, and stole business customers' contact details, ticket titles and some network IP addresses. It says no passwords were taken and services were not affected.
deck.whyItMatters: Telecom ticket data and circuit IPs are a map for follow-on phishing and network attacks; Bell's enterprise clients, including banks, should expect targeted lures.
deck.storyline: Storyline: big data breaches · day 6
deck.detailHtml: Bell Canada told BleepingComputer that on 17 Nov 'an agentic threat actor accessed some of our systems, including a system used for ordering and provisioning circuits, and exfiltrated some enterprise customer data'. The notice to customers says a pre-production copy of its Maximo system was reached and names, job titles, work emails, phone numbers, ticket titles and some network IP addresses may be exposed, but not credentials or attachments. Bell says services were not affected and it is sharing indicators with customers and Canada's cyber centre.

deck.headline: Signal blocks phone AI assistants from reading its chats on iOS and Android
deck.summary: Signal now blocks screenshots on iOS 27 and detects AI assistants reading the screen on Android, to stop agents such as Siri AI, Gemini and Meta's Muse capturing private chats. Users can turn it off. Signal says it cannot protect macOS and wants Apple, Google and Microsoft to give apps an opt-out.
deck.whyItMatters: Banking and payments apps face the same problem; if OS agents can read balances and one-time codes on screen, banks need the same opt-out Signal is asking for.
deck.storyline: Storyline: apps versus the AI built into phones · day 1
deck.detailHtml: Signal says it is now blocking screenshots in its app on iOS 27 and, on Android, switching protection on when it detects an AI assistant trying to read the screen. It names Apple's Onscreen Awareness for Siri AI, Google's Gemini Intelligence and third-party agents like Meta's Muse, which use accessibility permissions as 'a skeleton key'. Users can turn the protection off. Signal admits gaps: it cannot block Siri AI on macOS and some Android brands. It asks OS makers for a documented way for apps to opt out of AI data access.

deck.headline: Senate passes permitting bill that makes data centres pay for grid upgrades
deck.summary: The US Senate passed a bipartisan bill 62-33 to speed up approvals for power plants and power lines and to make data centres pay for the grid capacity and energy they use. Its future in the House is uncertain, as some Democrats say it weakens environmental protections.
deck.whyItMatters: If it becomes law, data-centre power costs rise and timelines shorten at once, changing the economics of every AI campus loan in the US.
deck.storyline: Storyline: building AI's power and data centres · day 30
deck.detailHtml: The Senate passed the Bipartisan American Affordability and Jobs Act by 62-33 on Thursday night (19 Nov), with 47 Republicans and 15 members of the Democratic caucus in favour (Utility Dive). It would shorten reviews for power plants, transmission lines and other energy infrastructure and 'make sure data centres pay for the energy they use' (AP via The Hindu). It was negotiated with the White House before the midterms; now some Democrats, including Georgia's Raphael Warnock, say it weakens environmental law and tribal and state authority, and its House path is uncertain.

deck.headline: Thinking Machines' Inkling 2 Mini loops its layers to reason better on a laptop
deck.summary: Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini, an open-weight model that runs its middle layers three times per token to reason better. It has 26.4B parameters, about 3.4B active, fits in about 20GB and runs on a laptop. The company says it leads open models under 100B on coding benchmarks.
deck.whyItMatters: A frontier-lab, laptop-sized coding model with open weights is a realistic option for banks that must keep code and data on-premises.
deck.storyline: Storyline: new kinds of AI models · day 9
deck.detailHtml: Thinking Machines released Inkling 2 Mini with open weights. It is a looped transformer: it runs its middle layers three times for every token, so it can 'reason longer without writing its reasoning down'. It has 26.4B parameters, 3.4B active (5.4B counting the loops), is trained mostly in NVFP4 and needs about 20GB, so it runs offline on a MacBook. The company says it leads open models under 100B on DeepSWE v1.1 (48.2%) and Vals Index v2.2 (46.5%); Artificial Analysis says it matches Qwen3.8 27B with about 5x fewer active parameters. It trails Qwen3.8-27B on multi-turn chat. A variable-loop research version is released too, because hidden looping can make a model's reasoning harder to monitor.

deck.headline: Architect Labs says its AI agents designed a new kind of CPU from scratch
deck.summary: Architect Labs says its AI agents designed Frostbite, a new kind of CPU, from the instruction set to the final chip layout, checking each part with formal proofs. It claims 4.59 times better performance per watt than a standard small core on 25 workloads. The chip has not been manufactured yet.
deck.whyItMatters: If AI can explore chip designs humans would not try, custom silicon gets cheaper and faster; until Frostbite is manufactured, treat the gain as a design-stage claim.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI building software by itself · day 4
deck.detailHtml: Architect Labs says Frostbite is 'a general-purpose CPU with a new instruction set' designed end-to-end by AI: its agent swarms iterated over the compiler, ISA, architecture, microarchitecture, RTL, verification and final GDS layout, with every block's contract checked in Lean. The chip runs interaction nets, where each computation step is local and has one owner, so parallel work comes 'straight from the program'. On 25 workloads, 15 held out until the end, it claims 4.59x performance per watt against a silicon-proven dual-issue in-order core. Its earlier AI-designed accelerator, Redwood, has so far run only on an FPGA (VentureBeat).

deck.headline: Researchers show a 27B model improving itself by editing its own weights
deck.summary: A new paper shows an open 27-billion-parameter model reading its own weights and graded answers, working out why it failed and editing the weights directly, with no training run. It gained 6.6 points on unseen problems and kept improving over eight sessions. Smaller models could not do it. Not yet peer reviewed.
deck.whyItMatters: A model that changes its own weights is harder to audit; model-risk teams should ask vendors whether deployed weights can change after validation.
deck.storyline: Storyline: AI building software by itself · day 4
deck.detailHtml: A paper on arXiv claims, 'to our knowledge for the first time', that a language model can rewrite its own weights by its own reasoning and get better, with no gradients and no training. An open 27B model, given its weights, graded answers and the ability to run itself, diagnoses its failures and edits the weights: it gains 6.6 points on problems it never saw, keeps improving over eight sessions, and restores a broken copy of itself to over 80% of the original accuracy. Smaller models in the same family either make no edit or break themselves.

deck.headline: OakNorth wins a US bank charter as Payoneer gets a nod for a stablecoin bank
deck.summary: UK business lender OakNorth now has a US national bank charter after regulators approved its purchase of a Michigan bank, so it can take deposits and offer payments. The US is already about 40% of its new lending. Payoneer separately says it has conditional approval for a stablecoin trust bank.
deck.whyItMatters: Fintech lenders and payments firms are turning into regulated US banks; incumbents should expect sharper competition for business deposits and cross-border payments.
deck.storyline: Storyline: fintechs becoming banks · day 1
deck.detailHtml: London-based OakNorth has a US national bank charter and is now a US bank holding company, after the Federal Reserve and OCC approved its purchase of Michigan-based Community Unity Bank (company release via PYMNTS). The US already accounts for about 40% of its new lending since it entered in 2023; it now plans checking and savings accounts, payments and accounting integrations for mid-market businesses. Separately, Payoneer announced OCC conditional approval for a national trust bank to issue a stablecoin, PAYO-USD (PR Newswire headline), joining MoonPay's application earlier this week.

deck.headline: Japan's biggest insurers see cyber claims triple as AI makes hacking easier
deck.summary: Japan's biggest insurers say cyber claims have surged: Tokio Marine got three times its usual number of claim notifications in October and Sompo 2.5 times its average, which they blame on AI-driven attacks. Both say losses remain within plan, but Tokio Marine may cap payouts or tighten terms.
deck.whyItMatters: The first hard claims data showing AI-era attacks hitting insurers; expect tighter cyber terms and higher premiums at renewals, including for banks.
deck.storyline: Storyline: cyber insurance and AI risk · day 2
deck.detailHtml: Tokio Marine received three times as many cyber-insurance claim notifications as usual in October, and Sompo's October claims ran 2.5 times its average for the year to September, the companies said at earnings briefings (Bloomberg via Insurance Journal). Both blame increasingly sophisticated AI-driven attacks. Sompo says inquiries about raising cover have tripled; Tokio Marine may cap payouts or tighten terms by risk profile but expects losses within plan. Only 8.8% of Japanese small businesses have cyber cover.

deck.headline: House report warns US firms off Chinese open models; Cursor may drop them
deck.summary: A House report calls US companies' use of Chinese open-weight AI models alarming, names Airbnb, DoorDash and Cursor's maker, and recommends barring such models from federal contracts and critical infrastructure. Cursor told lawmakers it may phase them out. OpenAI says it has cut attacks that copy its models' reasoning to under 1%.
deck.whyItMatters: Banks using Qwen, Kimi or DeepSeek derivatives, including inside vendor tools, should inventory them now; an AI bill of materials may become a procurement requirement.
deck.storyline: Storyline: US-China fights over AI models · day 4
deck.detailHtml: A 50-page report from the House Homeland Security and China Select committees warns that US companies embedding China-developed open-weight models risk a repeat of Huawei and ZTE, and names Airbnb, DoorDash and Cursor maker Anysphere (The Record). It makes 12 recommendations, including an American open-weight initiative, sourcing standards, an AI bill of materials, and barring Chinese models from federal contracts and critical infrastructure. Cursor told lawmakers it is considering phasing them out (CNBC headline). The same day OpenAI said it had cut successful attacks to extract GPT-6.2's hidden reasoning, a route to copying it, from 54% to under 1%.

deck.headline: Poland says a Russian cruise missile crashed on its soil during a NATO-allied drill
deck.summary: Poland says a Russian cruise missile crashed in a field about 50km from the Ukrainian border on Friday, along with a suspected second missile and a drone, during a huge Russian attack on Ukraine. Nobody was hurt. Prime Minister Tusk called it a provocation, and NATO scrambled jets.
deck.whyItMatters: A strike on NATO soil days after a peace-themed summit raises escalation risk; watch whether Poland invokes NATO consultations and how defence and European risk assets react on Monday.
deck.storyline: Storyline: Russian sabotage in Europe · day 2
deck.detailHtml: Poland's defence minister says a Russian Kh-101 cruise missile hit a rural area at Nowy Lipowiec, about 50km from the Ukrainian border, at about 06:30 on 20 Nov; a second suspected missile and a jet-powered drone also came down. Nobody was hurt (BBC). It happened during one of Russia's biggest air attacks on Ukraine of the war, a day after the Trump-Xi-Putin summit. PM Donald Tusk said it was 'no coincidence' the objects landed near an 11-nation 'coalition of the willing' exercise led by the UK and France. NATO scrambled jets; Secretary General Mark Rutte condemned 'grave violations'. Russia has not commented.

deck.whyItMatters: China's AI labs lose both imported chips and a manufacturing workaround; expect more reliance on domestic fabs and more pressure on Huawei and SMIC capacity.

deck.headline: Bitcoin drops to its lowest since September 2024 as $2bn of bets are wiped out
deck.summary: Bitcoin fell to $57,716 on Friday, its lowest price since September 2024, wiping out its gains since Trump's re-election as about $2 billion of leveraged bets were liquidated. Separately, tampered Ledger wallets sold by one reseller have been linked to $95 million in thefts.
deck.whyItMatters: Banks building stablecoin and custody businesses are doing so into a falling market; collateral haircuts on crypto-backed lending need checking.
deck.storyline: Storyline: money in and out of crypto · day 2
deck.detailHtml: Bitcoin fell to $57,716 intraday on 20 Nov, its lowest since September 2024, erasing every gain since Trump's re-election; about $2bn of leveraged long positions were liquidated in the previous 24 hours (Crypto Briefing). The whole crypto market was near $2.08 trillion, with ether around $1,624. It traded like a risk asset alongside the AI sell-off. Separately, a drainer campaign linked to Ledger hardware wallets sold by South-East Asian reseller CryptoBilis has taken $95.35m from 1,486 users by one tally; Tether froze $10m.
deck.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGCrypto Briefing: bitcoin falls to lowest since September 2024 · Crypto Briefing: Ledger users lose $95.35M in CryptoBilis-linked theft

alsoToday.headline: Open full-duplex voice model Haru-4B tops Hugging Face's trending list
alsoToday.summary: Haru-4B, from a little-known group called higurashi-ai, is an Apache 2.0 full-duplex speech-to-speech model: it can listen and speak at the same time, like a person on a phone call, in nine languages including English, Chinese and Japanese.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: An open, small duplex voice model makes in-house voice agents for call centres feasible without sending audio to a vendor.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: AI that listens and speaks · day 4
alsoToday.detailHtml: Haru-4B, from a little-known group called higurashi-ai, is an Apache 2.0 full-duplex speech-to-speech model: it can listen and speak at the same time, like a person on a phone call, in nine languages including English, Chinese and Japanese. Released on 12 Nov, it now leads Hugging Face's trending list with about 5,400 likes and 7,300 downloads. We have not seen independent tests.

alsoToday.headline: Databricks eyes $225bn and Cognition $75bn even as public AI stocks fall
alsoToday.summary: Databricks, whose software stores and analyses company data and builds AI apps, is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at about $225bn, up from $190bn in August; its Lakebase database has passed a $100m revenue run-rate (WSJ via Reuters).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Private marks are rising while public AI stocks fall; that gap is a valuation risk for funds and banks holding private AI exposure.
alsoToday.detailHtml: Databricks, whose software stores and analyses company data and builds AI apps, is in early talks to raise several billion dollars at about $225bn, up from $190bn in August; its Lakebase database has passed a $100m revenue run-rate (WSJ via Reuters). alsoToday.headline: Google's homepage drops the search button and adds an AI chat history
alsoToday.summary: Google's search VP Robby Stein confirmed a new desktop Google.com homepage that removes the 'Google Search' button and adds buttons for image generation, analysing files and brainstorming with Gemini. Signed-in users get an expandable sidebar of recent AI Mode conversations on the homepage and results page.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: The world's front door to the web now leads with AI chat; brands and banks that rely on search traffic should plan for answers that never send a click.

alsoToday.headline: Standard Bank automates its AI risk reviews, with humans keeping the final say
alsoToday.summary: Africa's largest lender, Standard Bank Group, built with AWS Professional Services an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own model-risk and change-risk policies. It produces reports and a dashboard showing what is in place and what needs mitigation, so the risk committee can approve faster; humans keep final approval.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: A copyable pattern for banks whose AI pipeline is stuck in risk review.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: how banks put AI to work · day 5
alsoToday.detailHtml: Africa's largest lender, Standard Bank Group, built with AWS Professional Services an automated assessment that scores each generative AI use case against international AI standards and its own model-risk and change-risk policies. It produces reports and a dashboard showing what is in place and what needs mitigation, so the risk committee can approve faster; humans keep final approval. The bank says it did not need a new AI policy, only a faster way to prove each system follows the existing one.

alsoToday.headline: Mastercard starts selling post-quantum readiness advice to banks
alsoToday.summary: Mastercard has launched a Quantum Advisory Practice covering cryptographic inventories, post-quantum migration strategies, remediation roadmaps and executive education, with a white paper on readiness. It is working with QIZ Security and Oxford Quantum Circuits, including a financial-fraud protection pilot (company release via The Quantum Insider).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: The card networks are turning post-quantum migration into a service; banks without a crypto inventory will be asked for one.

alsoToday.headline: Brazil's central bank sells $1bn to defend the real after Lula's re-election
alsoToday.summary: Brazil's central bank sold $1bn in a spot auction on 19 Nov, its first outright spot dollar sale since December 2024. The real has fallen from 5.00 to 5.94 per dollar since President Lula's surprise re-election in late October, as markets doubt he will put public finances on a sustainable path (Central Banking).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Latin America's biggest economy is under currency stress just as global risk appetite cracks; exposure to Brazilian corporates and FX hedges deserves a look.

alsoToday.headline: UK and EU agree a deal to cut food-trade red tape; Burnham wants closer ties
alsoToday.summary: The UK and EU agreed a deal on 20 Nov to cut checks and paperwork on food and agricultural trade, and Prime Minister Andy Burnham says the UK will explore even closer ties. M&S called it 'a major step forward' and Tesco 'good news for British farmers', but neither promised lower prices (BBC's Faisal Islam).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: The biggest post-Brexit reset so far; further steps on services and finance would matter more for UK banks.

alsoToday.headline: South Africa's ANC suffers its worst result since 1994 in local elections
alsoToday.summary: The ANC won 31% in this month's local elections, down from 46% in 2021 and its worst result since apartheid ended in 1994. It kept a majority in only Limpopo and came first in just two of eight big cities, against six in 2021.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Unstable coalitions in Johannesburg, Cape Town's neighbours and Durban affect municipal finances and the banks that lend to them.
alsoToday.detailHtml: The ANC won 31% in this month's local elections, down from 46% in 2021 and its worst result since apartheid ended in 1994. It kept a majority in only Limpopo and came first in just two of eight big cities, against six in 2021. It is racing to secure power-sharing deals but appears unwilling to copy its national coalition with the Democratic Alliance locally (BBC).
alsoToday.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGBBC: ANC fights to keep control of key cities

alsoToday.headline: Google signs a $500m-plus deal for 'superhot' geothermal power in Oregon
alsoToday.summary: Google will buy 50MW from Quaise Energy's Project Obsidian near Newberry Volcano, Oregon, to power its data centres in The Dalles from as early as 2030; Quaise values the deal at more than $500m. The first phase uses conventional drilling; a second uses millimetre-wave drilling to reach superhot rock (Utility Dive).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Big tech keeps underwriting unproven firm power; the drilling technology, not the contract, is the risk.

alsoToday.headline: FDA rejects Capricor's Duchenne cell therapy after two failed trials
alsoToday.summary: The FDA has rejected deramiocel, Capricor Therapeutics' cell therapy for Duchenne muscular dystrophy patients who can no longer walk. STAT says the decision 'should have been an easy one': Capricor ran two randomised trials and neither showed the therapy helped.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: A sign the FDA is holding the line on evidence even for rare diseases with few options.

alsoToday.headline: Five big drugmakers will stop new trials at Chinese military hospitals
alsoToday.summary: Merck, Eli Lilly, AbbVie, Pfizer and Bristol Myers Squibb told the House China Select Committee they will not open new clinical-trial sites in Xinjiang or at hospitals affiliated with the People's Liberation Army, after investigations into IP exposure and ethics opened in June (STAT).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: US-China decoupling is reaching drug development; trial costs and timelines for China-heavy programmes may rise.
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: the US-China biotech rivalry · day 1

alsoToday.whyItMatters: Bayern lose their top scorer for the title run-in and the Champions League knockouts.

alsoToday.headline: Waymo halts freeway rides nationwide and files a recall after California ban
alsoToday.summary: After California's DMV called Waymo's cars an 'imminent hazard' and barred them from state freeways, Waymo paused driverless freeway rides in all five markets that had them: the SF Bay Area, Los Angeles County, Phoenix, Miami and Austin (Scripps/CNN).
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Freeway access is what makes robotaxis viable for airport and commuter trips; the pause dents Waymo's lead just as Tesla pushes its Cybercab.
alsoToday.update: Waymo has paused freeway rides in all five markets that had them and has filed a recall over closed freeway lanes and manual traffic control (Reuters)
alsoToday.storyline: Storyline: robotaxis and self-driving cars · day 4
alsoToday.detailHtml: After California's DMV called Waymo's cars an 'imminent hazard' and barred them from state freeways, Waymo paused driverless freeway rides in all five markets that had them: the SF Bay Area, Los Angeles County, Phoenix, Miami and Austin (Scripps/CNN). The DMV cited 'recurrent incursions' into construction zones and a car that tried to pass a Highway Patrol traffic break. Reuters reports Waymo has now filed a recall over closed freeway lanes and manual traffic control; details are not yet on NHTSA's site.
alsoToday.sourcesHtml: REPORTINGScripps News: Waymo pauses all US freeway operations

alsoToday.headline: Rockstar says GTA VI made $3.79bn on day one, a record for any entertainment
alsoToday.summary: Rockstar Games says Grand Theft Auto VI earned $3.79bn in its first day, 'a new record for entertainment across any medium', and sold 32.5 million pre-orders (The Verge). That is well above the $2.36bn Sensor Tower estimate we carried yesterday.
alsoToday.whyItMatters: Take-Two now has hard numbers behind the launch; consumer spending held up even as markets fell.
alsoToday.update: Rockstar's own figure is $3.79bn on day one, well above the $2.36bn estimate we reported, with 32.5 million pre-orders
